item.title: How I Proved My Code Was Actually Running on Additional Propeller Cogs
item.content:encoded:
Using the linker map, worker-reported cog IDs, an LED runtime test, simulation and oscilloscope measurements

By Maryclare

My question was simple: How could I prove that code assigned to additional Propeller cogs was actually executing there, rather than merely existing somewhere in the compiled binary?

I was working with a Propeller 1 Demo Board, an older but unusual microcontroller built around multiple independent processors called cogs. Parallax lists the P8X32A as having eight 32-bit cores, 32 KB of shared hub RAM, and 512 32-bit words of local memory in each cog. This provides approximately 2 KB of local memory per cog.

The part that initially confused me was the relationship between the hub and the cogs. The hub stores shared program data and the compressed instruction stream. However, the hub does not execute instructions by itself. A cog still performs the processing. In my main program, Cog 0 ran the CMM kernel, which fetched and decompressed code stored in hub memory. The remaining cogs were available for worker code.

The PropGCC memory-model documentation explains that CMM stores code and data in hub memory and decompresses instructions through a runtime kernel. The mixed-mode documentation also explains that files ending in .cogc are compiled in the native COG memory model, even when the main project uses CMM. When a cog starts, it loads image it copied from hub memory into that cog’s local memory and execution begins there.

While working through the proofs, I realized that I needed evidence for these four claims:

· The worker cog images were included inside the hub.
· The main program successfully launched additional cogs other than cog 0.
· The worker code identified the cog it was running on (cog id or processor id).
· The worker paths continued executing at runtime on both the simulator and physical hardware.

1. Build evidence: the cog images existed in the linked program

I started with the linker map. The project contained two native worker modules: dummy.cogc and provecmm.cogc. The map file showed separate loadable sections for both images, including their sizes and hub load addresses.

This was necessary evidence, but it was not evidence that this file was running in a separate cog. The map only showed that the compiler and linker placed the worker images into the final program. A load image can exist without ever being launched on a cog because every instruction in the cmm memory model compiles the instructions to the hub but we want the cog instructions to run on other cogs like cog 1 and 2 while the main code runs on cog 0 to take advantage of the multiple cogs or processors . I therefore treated the map as the first layer of the proof, not the conclusion.

2. Launch evidence: the main cog started two workers

The GCC (PROPGCC) for propeller 1 generates external arrays that point to each. cogc image. The main program passed those arrays to cognew() along with pointers to the struct which holds variables :

extern unsigned int _load_start_dummy_cog[];
extern unsigned int _load_start_provecmm_cog[];

dummy_cog = cognew(_load_start_dummy_cog,
                   &dummy_data.mailbox);
monitor_cog = cognew(_load_start_provecmm_cog,
                     &monitor_data.mailbox);

In my terminal output, the main program reported Cog 0, then cognew() returned Cog 1 for the dummy worker and Cog 2 for the monitor worker. This showed that two additional cog slots had been allocated.

Worker code:

In the worker code the cog id was passed into the mailbox and called during run time, The main program then read and printed those mailbox values.

The dummy worker reported Cog 1, while the monitor worker reported Cog 2. Because cogid() was called inside the worker code, these values provided worker-side evidence of which cogs were executing the two worker images.

3. LED runtime evidence: the monitor worker toggled the Pin 20 LED

I performed a simpler physical runtime check with the Demo Board LED connected to Pin 20. This test used the provecmm.cogc monitor worker. Inside that worker, Pin 20 was configured as an output and toggled repeatedly. Because the Pin 20 output instruction was located inside the worker loop, the visible LED activity showed that the monitor worker had reached and continued executing that runtime path.

The code screenshot and board photograph below belong to this Pin 20 LED test.

4. Simulator evidence: Cogs 1 and 2 had active instruction states

I then ran the binary in SpinSim, stepped the execution 50,000 times, and requested the state of Cogs 0 through 3. The test deliberately included Cog 3 as an control test for an inactive cog.

{
 echo "verbose 0"
 for i in $(seq 1 50000); do echo "stepx"; done
 echo "state 0"
 echo "state 1"
 echo "state 2"
 echo "state 3"
 echo "exit"
 } | ./spinsim_new.exe -d cmm/provecmm.binary > cog_state_check.txt

The extracted trace repeatedly showed Cogs 1 and 2 executing waitcnt. Their state dumps contained nonzero program-counter and instruction values, while Cog 3 remained at zero with no wait flag set. SpinSim’s documentation describes its per-cog verbosity and state inspection features, which made it useful for comparing active and inactive cogs in the same run.

This simulator evidence helped separate “the program printed a cog number or just ran via just cog 0” from “the simulated processor state was actively advancing.”

Conclusion

To prove that a processor is running as it should, these are some basic tests I used.

My main verification method was:

check for the cog image → worker reports its own cog ID → the Pin 20 LED test confirms that the monitor worker reaches its runtime loop → SpinSim shows active cog state.

The appendix records a separate Pin 2 oscilloscope built as additional physical evidence that a. cogc worker can repeatedly execute an instrumented output path.

If there are any limitations or suggestions, feedback would be highly appreciated.

Appendix: Separate Pin 2 oscilloscope test

For a separate physical-output check, I compiled a test .cogc file specifically for oscilloscope observation. In this build, the worker configured Pin 2 as an output, set Pin 2 HIGH immediately before writing pressure = 123 and new_sample = 1, waited, and then set Pin 2 LOW. The HIGH-LOW loop repeated continuously. Because this was a separate test program, I have kept it in the appendix rather than presenting it as part of the exact same run as the main verification.

Any code that writes to an input output pin will do for the oscilloscope test just make sure it writes from the cog. So the provecmm code would have worked the same just change led 20 to pin 2(or any input/output pin ).

Sources and code

· Parallax Propeller 1 overview

· P8X32A Propeller Datasheet

· PropGCC documentation: Memory Models

· PropGCC documentation: In-Depth and Mixed-Mode Programming

· SpinSim documentation

All code and supporting files for the experiment are collected in one public GitHub repository. Open the repository first, then use the file guide below to find the evidence or test discussed in each section.

· GitHub repository: maryclareok/propellercogproof

Abbreviations:

CMM: Compact Memory Model

COG: Parallax’s term for one of the Propeller microcontroller’s independent processor cores

GCC: GNU Compiler Collection

item.title: One Prompt vs Six: I Ran Two AI Builders in Parallel at a Hackathon
item.content:encoded:
A real build log from PromptWars (Google for Developers): autonomous agent vs spec-first workflow, how each one handled rate limits differently, and the exact prompts I used — word for word.

SEO description: A real, solo hackathon case study comparing an autonomous coding agent (Hermes + Nemotron 3 Ultra) against a spec-first Claude-to-Antigravity workflow — with exact prompts, architecture diagrams, how both agents handled 429s during code generation differently, and the one mistake that cost a ranking at a 93% score.

The Setup: One Person, Two AI Builders, Running at the Same Time

This was a solo, in-person hackathon — PromptWars, hosted by Google for Developers — so there was no team, no division of labor, just me and a 3-hour clock. The brief: Destination Discovery & Cultural Experiences.

Build a GenAI-powered platform that helps travelers discover destinations and engage with local culture in meaningful ways. The solution must use Generative AI to recommend attractions, uncover hidden gems, generate immersive storytelling, promote heritage, suggest local events, and connect visitors with authentic cultural experiences.

No mock data. Everything real, everything connected.

I want to be upfront about what I actually did, because the honest version is more useful than a clean narrative: I didn’t run one approach, watch it fail, and then switch to another. I ran two things in parallel.

I gave the Hermes agent — using Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B model for reasoning via an Nvidia API key — a single prompt: just the raw challenge text, pasted as-is, nothing more. Hermes started working on its own from that one prompt. While it was running, I switched over and started refining prompts through Claude and feeding the refined specs into Gemini IDE’s Antigravity, iterating there.

About 45 minutes in, after a few iterations, Antigravity showed me a working UI with services actually integrated and calling real APIs. Hermes, meanwhile, was still running — still reasoning, still working through the problem with Nemotron 3 Ultra underneath it.

I want to be honest that this isn’t an apples-to-apples comparison. Hermes got one short prompt and had to infer almost everything itself(past skills and my interaction learning). Antigravity got a much more detailed, iteratively-refined spec, developed through several rounds with Claude. That’s not a fair fight in either direction — it’s closer to two different questions: “what can an agent do with almost nothing” versus “what can a code-gen IDE do when it’s handed a real spec.”

How each agent handled 429s during code generation

This is worth being precise about, because the difference is meaningful.

Both agents hit 429 quota-exceeded errors during the code-writing phase — not in the final app, but while the AI was actively generating code and calling the Gemini API to do so.

Hermes hit these 429s during its own reasoning loop and recovered autonomously. It self-detected the rate limit, backed off, and kept working — all from the single original prompt, with no intervention from me. That’s genuinely autonomous agent behaviour.

Antigravity had a general error-detection and self-fixing loop, which worked well for most issues during code generation. But for 429 specifically — detecting rate-limit errors and implementing backoff in the generated code itself — that wasn’t automatic. I had to write and send a dedicated rate-limit prompt to get that behaviour explicitly. The general error loop was there; the 429-specific backoff needed its own spec.

This is a meaningful distinction: Hermes’s autonomous recovery from 429 during code generation versus Antigravity needing an explicit spec for it is the clearest evidence that the two approaches differ fundamentally in how much they need from you.

Repo submitted for Hermes / Nemotron 3 Ultra attempt: github.com/karangehlod/cultural-travel-companion

The Hermes + Nemotron 3 Ultra (550B-A55B) run, working from a single pasted prompt — no follow-up iteration, no refinement.

The build I actually submitted to the hackathon was the Claude-to-Antigravity one — TravelYarro — and that repo, promptwars-indore, is the final submission.

Live app: travelyarro.web.app
Submitted repo: github.com/karangehlod/promptwars-indore
Hermes repo: https://github.com/karangehlod/cultural-travel-companion

Stack: Vite + React 19 + TypeScript (strict) + Tailwind + Zustand + Zod + @google/generative-ai, client-only, deployed to Firebase Hosting.

Tech Stack: What I Picked and Why

Every choice here was made against a 3-hour clock as a solo builder, not against a “what’s technically best” standard.

Architecture: Two Very Different Mental Models

Before the prompts, it helps to see what each approach actually looks like structurally.

Hermes (Nemotron 3 Ultra) — Autonomous agent loop

TravelYarro (Claude → Antigravity) — Spec-first iterative pipeline

TravelYarro internal application architecture

The core idea: nothing above the provider layer knows or cares whether it’s talking to real Gemini or a test mock. Adding an 8th feature later is a new service file plus one line in the facade — zero edits to anything else.

The Prompts I Actually Used, Word for Word

1. The Hermes Prompt (single prompt, no follow-up)

This is the entire input Hermes got — the raw challenge text, pasted once:

Destination Discovery & Cultural Experience as the Topic
3 submission attempt and here is detail.
[full brief text as shown in the hackathon brief]
we will use AI features in it no mock data everything should be real and connected

That’s it — one prompt, and Hermes started working from there entirely on its own reasoning. It hit 429 errors during code generation and recovered without any input from me.

2. Master Antigravity Build Spec (Claude-refined, sent to Antigravity first)

MASTER PROMPT — AntiGravity Build Spec: "Culturo" AI Travel Companion
STACK: Vite + React 18 + TypeScript (strict) + Tailwind CSS + Zustand + Zod + @google/generative-ai (client-only, no backend). Deploy target: Netlify/Firebase Hosting, single command.
═══════════════════════════════════════
0. GLOBAL RULES
═══════════════════════════════════════
- TypeScript strict mode, no `any`, no implicit returns. Every AI response validated with Zod before touching state.
- Two Gemini models via env vars (VITE_GEMINI_API_KEY):
  • FAST_MODEL = "gemini-2.5-flash" → recommendations, hidden gems, heritage, events, experiences (5 parallel structured JSON calls, low latency needed)
  • DEEP_MODEL = "gemini-2.5-pro" → storytelling (narrative quality) and itinerary generation (multi-step reasoning, budget math)
  Store model names in `services/config.ts`, never hardcode inline.
- All Gemini calls use `responseMimeType: "application/json"` + explicit JSON schema in the prompt; parse → Zod.safeParse → on fail: 1 retry with "STRICT JSON ONLY, no markdown" appended, then surface typed error.
- Every async feature has 3 UI states: loading (skeleton), error (retry button), success. No bare spinners.
- Global ErrorBoundary at App root; local error boundaries per dashboard panel so one failed AI call doesn't kill the page.
- Theme: Tailwind `darkMode: 'class'`, CSS variables for surface/text/accent, toggle persisted to localStorage, system-preference default.
- Responsive: mobile-first, stacked single column <768px, grid 2–3 col ≥1024px.
- Tests: Vitest + React Testing Library. Unit tests for Zod schemas + agent.ts parsers (mock fetch). Minimum: 1 test file per service function, 1 per stateful component.
[...remaining spec sections: FILE TREE, TYPES/ENTITIES, AGENT.TS, BUILD ORDER, ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA - see GitHub repo for full text]

3. TravelYarro v2 — UI/UX Polish + Clean Architecture (SOLID refactor)

(Applies on top of the master spec — renames the app to TravelYarro, adds Framer Motion, enforces class-based SOLID architecture with IAIProvider interface, GeminiProvider, MockProvider, and 7 domain services.)

4. State Persistence Spec

(Adds localStorage hydration, prevents re-triggering AI calls on refresh, deep state persistence across page reload.)

5. Fix Gemini 429 Rate Limit + Improve UX

This is the prompt I had to write explicitly because Antigravity’s general error-fixing loop didn’t cover 429s automatically during code generation:

Fix Gemini 429 Rate Limit + Improve UX (Loading + Retry + Animations)
You are a senior frontend engineer working on a Vite + React + TypeScript application using Gemini.
The app is currently failing with repeated 429 quota exceeded errors and poor UX during AI calls.
Your job is to fix API abuse, implement proper rate-limit handling, and upgrade the UX with smooth
loading states and animations.
[Rate limit handling: request deduplication, exponential backoff at 2s/5s/10s with max 3 retries,
 user-facing error states, global AI lock, skeleton loaders, step-based loading copy for each
 AI pipeline stage - see GitHub repo for full text]

6. README + Setup + Firebase Deployment Guide

(Generates a production-ready README covering local setup, Firebase CLI steps, env vars, common issues, and scripts. See repo for full text.)

The 8-Step Build Order (From the Master Spec)

The prompt above specifies a strict sequence, and I followed it as written:

Step 1 — Foundation. Vite scaffold, Tailwind dark-mode config, Zustand store skeleton, every TypeScript type and Zod schema up front, a mock Gemini client behind VITE_USE_MOCKS. Types drive everything downstream, so this had to come first.

Step 2 — ProfileWizard. A 4-step form (Interests → Budget/Style → Dates/Pace → Dietary/Accessibility), Zod-validated per step, no advancing on incomplete data.

Step 3 — DestinationInput. City/region input plus a date range picker. Submitting fires 5 parallel Gemini calls via Promise.allSettled, so no single failure blocks the rest.

Step 4 — Parallel AI Dashboard. Five independent panels, each with its own loading → error-with-retry → success state, and an “add to trip” toggle per card.

Step 5 — StorytellingModal. Streamed narrative generation, token-by-token rendering, a theme selector that re-triggers generation.

Step 6 — ItineraryBuilder. Shows selections and running budget; “Generate Itinerary” calls the deep model with full day-by-day reasoning.

Step 7 — ItineraryView + PDF Export. Timeline layout, budget breakdown, html2canvas + jsPDF export.

Step 8 — Polish. Error boundaries, toast system, dark/light contrast audit, responsive audit, Lighthouse pass — deliberately last, only after core flows worked.

Gemini API Rate Limiting: The Agent-Level and App-Level Story

There are two distinct 429 stories in this build, and it’s worth separating them clearly.

429s during code generation (agent level)

Both Hermes and Antigravity hit rate-limit errors while writing code — the AI coding agent itself was calling the Gemini API and occasionally getting throttled.

  • Hermes hit these and recovered autonomously, from just the one prompt. No input from me. Self-detected, backed off, continued.
  • Antigravity had a general error-detection and self-fixing loop that caught most issues during code generation. For 429s specifically — detecting the rate-limit error and writing proper backoff logic into the generated code — it needed an explicit spec (prompt #5 above). The loop was there; the 429-aware behaviour inside it needed to be asked for.

429s in the final app (runtime level)

Once the code was generated, the deployed app also needed 429 handling for its own Gemini API calls. This came from the explicit rate-limit prompt. The three-layer strategy:

1. Request deduplication

const requestCache = new Map<string, Promise<unknown>>();
async function cachedCall<T>(key: string, fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  if (requestCache.has(key)) return requestCache.get(key) as Promise<T>;
  const promise = fn();
  requestCache.set(key, promise);
  promise.finally(() => requestCache.delete(key));
  return promise;
}

2. Exponential backoff on 429

// Exact delays as documented: 2s, 5s, 10s
const RETRY_DELAYS = [2000, 5000, 10000];
async function retryWithBackoff<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= RETRY_DELAYS.length; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (err: any) {
      const is429 = err?.status === 429;
      const hasRetry = attempt < RETRY_DELAYS.length;
      if (is429 && hasRetry) {
        await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, RETRY_DELAYS[attempt]));
      } else {
        throw err;
      }
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
Note on Gemini free-tier rate limits: The free tier is per model, not a single shared cap. Gemini 2.5 Flash (used for the 5 parallel dashboard calls) gets 10 RPM on the free tier. Gemini 2.5 Pro (used for storytelling and itinerary) gets 5 RPM. The common claim that all models cap at “5 RPM” understates the actual Flash limit.

3. User-facing error state

{error?.status === 429 && (
  <div className="bg-amber-50 border border-amber-200 p-4 rounded-lg">
    <p className="text-amber-900 font-medium">You've hit the AI usage limit.</p>
    <p className="text-sm text-amber-700 mt-1">Please wait ~30 seconds and try again.</p>
    <button onClick={retry} className="mt-3 px-4 py-2 bg-amber-600 text-white rounded text-sm">
      Retry
    </button>
  </div>
)}

Result: zero 429 errors in the shipped demo path.

State Persistence: Solving Zero Data Loss

import { debounce } from 'lodash-es';
// On app load - hydrate before rendering
useEffect(() => {
  const saved = localStorage.getItem('travelyarro-state');
  if (saved) {
    const state = JSON.parse(saved);
    useAppStore.setState(state);
    console.log('[INIT] State restored from localStorage');
  }
}, []);
// On every state change - debounced save
const saveState = debounce((state: AppState) => {
  const toSave = {
    profile: state.profile,
    selections: state.selections,
    itinerary: state.itinerary,
    // NO API keys, NO secrets
  };
  localStorage.setItem('travelyarro-state', JSON.stringify(toSave));
  console.log('[STORE] Persisted to localStorage');
}, 2000);
// Zustand subscribe - correct API (no options object)
const unsubscribe = useAppStore.subscribe(saveState);
The state restores in under 100ms, with no visible flicker, and — per the spec — never re-triggers the AI pipeline automatically.

UI Polish Without Complexity

Skeleton loaders (no layout shift during loading):

function CardSkeleton() {
  return <div className="rounded-lg bg-gray-200 h-40 animate-pulse" />;
}

Step-based loading copy (travel-specific, not generic):

{step === 'recommendations' && <p className="text-sm text-gray-500">Finding top recommendations...</p>}
{step === 'gems' && <p className="text-sm text-gray-500">Uncovering hidden gems...</p>}
{step === 'heritage' && <p className="text-sm text-gray-500">Loading heritage insights...</p>}
{step === 'events' && <p className="text-sm text-gray-500">Checking local events...</p>}
{step === 'experiences' && <p className="text-sm text-gray-500">Finding authentic experiences...</p>}

Card entrance animation (Framer Motion):

<motion.div
  initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 20 }}
  animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}
  transition={{ type: 'spring', stiffness: 120, damping: 16 }}
>
  {/* Card content */}
</motion.div>

Testing: What the Specs Actually Required

describe('RecommendationService', () => {
  it('builds valid prompt including profile context', () => {
    const prompt = buildPrompt({ interests: ['food', 'history'], budget: { level: 'mid' } });
    expect(prompt).toContain('food');
    expect(prompt).toContain('history');
  });
  it('validates response against Zod schema', () => {
      const result = recommendationSchema.safeParse(mockRecommendations);
      expect(result.success).toBe(true);
    });
  });
  describe('ItineraryBuilder', () => {
    it('disables generate button until ≥1 selection', () => {
      render(<ItineraryBuilder selections={[]} />);
      expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /generate/i })).toBeDisabled();
    });
  });

Live Proof

The Numbers

The Score, and the One Prompt I Didn’t Write

I scored 93% on the hackathon’s evaluation criteria. Every criterion I actually wrote a spec for came through cleanly: architecture, feature completeness, rate-limit handling, state persistence, documentation.

The one thing that cost me a ranking wasn’t a bug — it was an omission. I never wrote an explicit code-quality prompt into the initial spec set. Architecture, UX polish, persistence, rate limiting, and documentation all got their own dedicated prompt. Code quality as a category — consistent formatting rules, linting thresholds, complexity limits, naming conventions enforced up front — didn’t. It came through incidentally, as a side effect of the SOLID/DRY architecture spec, but it was never its own explicit ask.

That’s the actual lesson: write a spec for every axis you’ll be judged on, not just the ones that feel like obvious engineering problems.

What We Deliberately Didn’t Build (And Why)

Verdict: Which Approach Wins Where

Both are genuinely useful. The difference isn’t capability — it’s input quality and time horizon. The autonomous agent shines when you can let it run. The spec-first workflow shines when you have a rubric and a clock.

Five Things Worth Stealing for Your Next Build

1. Specs beat code, every time you’re under a deadline. Even a rough bullet-point spec buys back debugging time — the ratio held across all five prompts here.

2. Build order prevents thrashing. Foundation → profile → destination → dashboard meant no mid-build refactors; each step could trust the previous one worked.

3. Architecture patterns compound. SOLID + Facade meant every new AI feature was a new, isolated, independently-testable domain service, with zero blast radius on existing code.

4. Rate limiting is two separate problems. First: will your code-generation agent hit 429s during the build and recover? (Hermes: autonomous. Antigravity: needs a spec.) Second: will your finished app hit 429s at runtime? Both need explicit planning — one at build time, one in your codebase.

5. Write a spec for every axis you’ll be scored on — including implicit ones. Code quality specifically needs its own ask. Don’t assume it rides along with architecture. 93% proves “mostly” and “entirely” are not the same thing.

Try It Yourself

  • Live app: travelyarro.web.app
  • Submitted repo (Claude specs → Antigravity build): github.com/karangehlod/promptwars-indore
  • Comparison run (Hermes + Nemotron 3 Ultra, single prompt): github.com/karangehlod/cultural-travel-companion

The Real Takeaway

I didn’t submit TravelYarro because it was the faster or smarter build. I submitted it because the specs created clarity, the architecture prevented chaos, the tests gave me confidence to deploy without fear, and the rate limiting — at both the agent level and the runtime level — was planned rather than bolted on.

93% says the approach mostly worked. The missing code-quality prompt says “mostly” is the whole game.

item.title: Why Neural Processing Units are Shaping the Future of Edge AI
item.content:encoded:
The role of NPUs in powering the future of edge devices.

Everybody already knows that artificial intelligence is no longer just an academic term, much less a momentary hype.

Several industries have already been revolutionized, especially due to applications powered by generative models such as the Large Language Models (LLMs).

However, there’s still a challenging dilemma when it comes to making these products scalable and profitable: computational cost. Companies like OpenAI, for example, spend millions of dollars just to maintain the infrastructure behind complex models such as GPT-5.

One of the strategies to reduce the demand for expensive servers is to decentralize processing into smaller, and sometimes even better, models for specific tasks, called Small Language Models (SLMs).

Still, even the most optimized SMLs have a high computational cost, particularly for edge devices such as smartphones and laptops.

For this reason, NPUs have become increasingly popular in the market, thanks to their ability to handle deep learning workloads, focusing primarily on energy efficiency.

Microsoft itself, in an attempt to boost the adoption of this technology, created the “Copilot+” label for devices capable of running AI locally.

With that in mind, this article aims to explore the practical advantages of using an NPU for complex AI tasks, as well as compare its performance against more common hardware components like GPUs and CPUs.

What are NPUs

Before diving into more technical details, let's define what exactly a Neural Processing Unit is.

In simple terms, NPUs are a type of “application-specific integrated circuit”, meaning a hardware component designed for a very specific purpose. Because of that specialization, these chips can deliver higher performance while consuming less energy.

In this way, NPUs were created to accelerate real-time AI workloads, mainly focused on edge devices, where the energy consumption must be as low as possible.

Why use NPUs in our daily lives?

Nowadays, we're increasingly surrounded by applications that rely on AI models, such as voice assistants, video conferencing apps, translation and transcription tools, and so on.

Let's consider a video call on Google Meet as an example. When you use a blur effect to hide your background, this task can be easily handled by the device's GPU or even its CPU (which is more common for this application).

On the other hand, we all know that, unfortunately, video meetings can last much longer than an hour. Executing this task on a less efficient device, like a CPU, causes the device to consume more power and, consequently, generate more heat (something you've probably already noticed in practice). This effect is especially undesirable when you're using a device that relies on a battery.

That's where NPUs come into play. By offloading AI-specific tasks to a dedicated chip, they not only considerably reduce energy consumption and heat but also make it possible to run more complex models.

Back to the video call example, you've probably noticed that blur and background replacement aren't perfect, sometimes leaving parts of the background visible and creating image artifacts.

That happens because companies need to limit the complexity of the executed models in order to reduce computational cost and ensure compatibility with as many devices as possible.

With specialized hardware like NPUs, developers can deploy more advanced and useful models in their applications. Some segmentation models, for example, are capable of replacing your background as if you were using a green screen.

Finally, another advantage of NPUs is to reduce the load on the other components of your device. Even a relatively simple model can consume over 30% of the available CPU, overloading the chip and reducing the performance on other parallel tasks. By distributing the workload, NPUs improve the overall efficiency of the device.

NPU limitations

Even though NPUs are very useful, some important limitations need to be mentioned. The main one is related to performance, as this device stands out for its energy cost-benefit, but not necessarily for delivering huge computational power.

Therefore, GPUs are still much more recommended for training and inference tasks of very complex models.

The number of TOPs (Trillions of Operations per Second) is the metric adopted by industry to measure the computational power of a component in processing AI tasks.

That said, while the most advanced NPU currently available can reach around 45 TOPs, high-end graphics cards like the Nvidia RTX 4090 can surpass 1,300 TOPs.

It makes it clear that NPUs are not meant to replace GPUs in all segments. Instead, their role is to enable the execution of AI workloads locally on certain devices.

What about TPUs?

If you’ve been studying AI for a while, you may have come across TPUs (Tensor Processing Units). Although TPUs are similar to NPUs in the sense that they're also specialized hardware for AI workloads, they are even more specific, designed primarily to accelerate neural networks and tensor computations.

Unlike NPUs, TPUs can even surpass the computational capacity of GPUs in some inference tasks and AI model training.

Still, these chips haven’t gained as much mainstream attention because they're tailored to specific models and frameworks, making them less ideal for general-purpose use.

On top of that, TPUs are a Google-developed solution that isn’t embedded into edge devices. Instead, the company offers TPU-based servers as part of its cloud services.

Executing a model on NPU

To test the NPU's capabilities in practice, let's run YOLOV5, one of the most popular object detection models, presenting a great balance between accuracy and computational cost. More specifically, we will use the "M" version, which has 21.2 million parameters.

For this test, I'll be using the NPU integrated into my Intel Core Ultra 5 245k processor, which, according to the manufacturer, can reach up to 13 TOPs of processing power.

It's also worth mentioning that, just like happens with CPUs and GPUs, software and framework compatibility may vary depending on the chip manufacturer. In the case of Intel's NPU, the most common toolkit for running inferences is OpenVino, although other frameworks are also supported.

Converting the trained model

The first required step is to convert the trained model to a suitable format. As previously mentioned, we will use OpenVino to execute model inference and interact with our Intel hardware (NPU and CPU).

Therefore, we need to convert YoloV5 from its original Pytorch (.pt) format into OpenVINO IR format. This proprietary format splits the model into two files, an .xml file, which contains the model topology, and a .bin file, which stores the weights.

The OpenVino documentation provides several examples of how to convert models from various frameworks, including PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Keras. In my case, the best approach was to perform the following conversions:

  • Pytorch -> ONNX -> OpenVino IR

ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is an open format used to define machine learning models through a common representation of operators and building blocks.

The goal of ONNX is to give developers the flexibility to train models in different frameworks and tools while maintaining interoperability between them.

Converting YoloV5 to ONNX is straightforward, since the official repository already includes a built-in export utility. To do so, first, it's necessary to clone the Git repository:

git clone https://github.com/ultralytics/yolov5.git

After that, inside the repository root, run:

python export.py --weights yolov5m.pt --img 640 --include onnx
You will likely need to install some dependencies on your machine for these commands to work, such as Pytorch itself, for example.

If everything runs successfully, you should see the yolov5m.onnx file created in the directory. Finally, use OpenVINO’s built-in conversion utility to transform the ONNX model into its IR format:

python -m openvino.tools.ovc .\yolov5m.onnx --output_model yolov5m.xml --compress_to_fp16

After running the command, you’ll have the .xml and .bin files that make up your OpenVino IR model.

Running inference with the model

Now that we have a supported model, we just need to load it into memory and use it to perform inferences, which is pretty much the same as any other deep learning model running on CPU or GPU.

The snippet below shows how to load OpenVino IR models:

import openvino as ov

core = ov.Core()
compiled_model = core.compile_model(
    "model_path", 'NPU')
output_layer = compiled_model.output(0)
All the source code examples displayed in this article are available on GitHub.

Afterwards, we need to create a function responsible for loading an image and applying some preprocessing, ensuring that we are using the same resolution expected by the model, in addition to normalizing the values between 0 and 1 and formatting the dimensions of the input data:

import cv2
import numpy as np

def preprocess_image(image):
    img_input = cv2.resize(image, (640, 640))
    img_input = cv2.cvtColor(img_input, cv2.COLOR_RGB2BGR)
    img_input = img_input.transpose((2, 0, 1))
    img_input = np.expand_dims(
        img_input, axis=0).astype(np.float32) / 255.0
    return img_input

image = cv2.imread("my_image.jpg")
original_height, original_width = image.shape[:2]

input_data = preprocess_image(image.copy())

Lastly, we perform inferences and draw the bounding boxes on the image:

result = compiled_model([input_data])[output_layer] # model inference

pred = result.squeeze(0)
boxes = non_max_suppression_opencv(
    [pred], 0.4, 0.45)

scale_x = original_width / 640 # Adjusting image scale.
scale_y = original_height / 640

for box in boxes:
    x1, y1, x2, y2, score, cls_id = box

    x1 = int(x1 * scale_x)
    y1 = int(y1 * scale_y)
    x2 = int(x2 * scale_x)
    y2 = int(y2 * scale_y)

    label = f"{int(cls_id)} {score:.2f}"
    cv2.rectangle(image, (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (0, 255, 0), 5)
    cv2.putText(image, label, (x1, y1 - 10),
                cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.6, (0, 0, 255), 5)

cv2.imwrite('output_image.jpg', image)

If everything worked correctly, you should see the model’s output generated directly by the NPU:

Practical benchmarking: CPU vs GPU vs NPU

Finally, let's jump into the most interesting part: what's the practical difference when running the same deep learning model on CPU, GPU, and NPU?

To do this comparison, I used a sample video of people walking down the street and measured the average Frames Per Second (FPS) that the model could achieve on each hardware component.

In this case, the source code is a little bit longer, as it involves creating a Python class to read the video frames and queue them, along with preprocessing, inference, and calculating the average FPS. For this reason, I'll leave those details aside, which will be available on the GitHub repository.

The most important aspect here is that I used OpenVino to run the model on both CPU and NPU, and Pytorch for GPU execution, since my graphics card isn't supported by Intel's framework.

Once again, this is my hardware configuration for this benchmarking:

  • Processor: Intel Core Ultra 5 245k.
  • NPU: Intel (13 TOPs of processing power).
  • Graphics card: Nvidia RTX 3060.

Another interesting metric to consider in this benchmark is the energy efficiency of each component. However, accurately measuring energy consumption can be tricky, as there are several operating system subprocesses running simultaneously, which can interfere with the readings.

Still, I used the HWMonitor software to get an approximate average of how many watts (W) each component was demanding while running the model.

Results on CPU

Let’s start with the CPU, which is the least suitable component for this type of workload, given its limitations in handling the highly parallel computations required for deep learning inference.

Even so, in many scenarios, running a model on the CPU is the only available option, as some devices don't have a dedicated hardware component to execute this task.

That said, the obtained results are shown below:

As expected, the CPU was not able to deliver satisfactory performance, reaching an average of only 6.10 FPS. Besides that, the processor usage was extremely high during model inference, with power consumption reaching around 100 W.

Results on GPU

The GPUs, on the other hand, are the standard device used by most servers and infrastructures dedicated to AI applications. This is due to their capability to process massive parallel computations and matrix operations, which are essential for deep learning inference.

This is one of the reasons why NVIDIA, the world’s leading GPU provider, has become the most valuable tech company in the world.

Here are the results:

It's easy to notice the difference in video smoothness, reaching an average of 54.5 FPS during inference. In addition, the average GPU power consumption was 87.3 W.

You might be wondering why energy consumption was actually lower than on the CPU. While GPUs typically draw more power, in this particular case, the inference workload was considerably less demanding for the GPU compared to the CPU.

While the task manager showed over 50% of CPU utilization, the GPU was running at less than 35% of its capacity, which resulted in lower energy consumption.

Results on NPU

Finally, let's evaluate the performance of this neural chip that was specifically designed for AI workloads:

This time, the model inference reached an average of 22.3 FPS. Furthermore, the processor, which is integrated with NPU, recorded an average power consumption of only 35 W.

As expected, the NPU is not able to reach the same processing power as the GPU. However, its main advantage lies in its energy efficiency, as the chip was able to deliver approximately 3.6 times more performance than the CPU, consuming only a third of the energy.

Results summary

The following table provides a comparative overview of the performance across different hardware components when running the deep learning model:

Conclusion

With the rise of artificial intelligence, it's not only software and new models that matter. Choosing the right hardware to perform each type of task is extremely important, especially for edge devices, which face greater computing capacity constraints.

While GPUs will likely remain the primary choice for large-scale training and inference workloads, NPUs are expected to gain popularity. This is particularly true as companies follow the trend of decentralizing AI processing, moving part of the workloads directly to end-user devices.

In this context, local processing is becoming an increasingly viable alternative, driven by the emergence and rapid evolution of specialized chips.

This change may represent not only significant efficiency gains but also competitive advantages for organizations that know how to leverage these resources, enabling the creation of new AI-powered products and services at the edge.

item.title: Agentic AI with LangChain — Part 1: Building A Semantic RAG Pipeline
item.content:encoded:
This article kicks off my Agentic AI with LangChain series. In this part, we build a complete, production‑style Semantic RAG pipeline that supports PDF uploads, processes documents into vector embeddings, and answers user questions through an interactive chatbot interface.

You will see the full workflow end‑to‑end:

  • uploading PDF files
  • extracting and cleaning text
  • splitting content into semantically meaningful chunks
  • generating embeddings
  • ingesting data into Pinecone
  • retrieving context using vector similarity
  • exposing FastAPI endpoints for ingestion and Q&A
  • connecting a Streamlit chatbot frontend

By the end, you’ll have a fully functioning RAG system that lets you upload PDFs as a knowledge base and query them through a conversational UI. Code of this article is available in this GitHub Repo.

🧰 Tech Stack

  • LangChain Expression Language (LCEL): LLM chains
  • OpenAI gpt‑4o‑mini: embeddings + generation
  • Pinecone: vector storage + retrieval
  • FastAPI : backend ingestion + Q&A
  • Streamlit: chatbot frontend
  • Python: glue for the entire pipeline

1. System Configurations

Create a .env file in the project root and define all required API keys:

OPENAI_API_KEY="<Your OpenAI API Key>"
VECTOR_DB=pinecone
Hugging_Face_TOKEN=<your huggingface token>
PINECONE_API_KEY=<your Pinecone API Key>
PINECONE_ENVIRONMENT=gcp-starter
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT="https://api.smith.langchain.com"
LANGSMITH_API_KEY="<Your LangSmith API Key"
LANGSMITH_PROJECT="agent-ai"
TAVILY_API_KEY=<Your TAVILY API Key>

Load these variables using a Pydantic BaseSettings class:

class BaseConfig(BaseSettings):
    OPENAI_API_KEY: Optional[str]
    PINECONE_API_KEY: Optional[str]
    TAVILY_API_KEY: Optional[str]

    """Loads the dotenv file. Including this is necessary to get
    pydantic to load a .env file."""
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", extra="ignore")

2. Project Structure

project/
├── rag_process/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── extractor.py
|   └── service.py
│       
├── chains.py           # llm chains
├── nodes.py            # python functions utlizing llm chains
|── schemas.py          # pydantic data models 
|── upload.py           # python functions to upload files asynchronously
├── main.py             # fastAPI app 
├── config.py           # pydantic BaseConfig
│── dependencies.py     # dependency inject to fastAPI endpoint function
├── test_chains.py      # pytests
├── .env                # environment variable definition
├── client.py           # streamlit client           
├── .gitignore
└── requirements.txt     # package requirements

The project is organized around four core components:

2.1. LLM chains

  • chains.py: LCEL chains
  • nodes.py: functions that invoke chains

2.2. Symantic RAG

  • rag_process/: extraction, splitting, ingestion, retrival

2.3. FastAPI Backend

  • upload.py, schema.py, dependencies.py, main.py

2.4. Streamlit client

  • client.py: chatbot UI

3. LLM Chains with LCEL

3.1. LangChain Expression Language (LCEL)

LCEL lets you build LLM pipeline using a clean, declarative syntax:

prompt | model | output_parser

Each stage transforms the input and passes it forward. This makes multi-step logic easy to read and maintain.

Example: Document Relevance Grader

class GradeDocuments(BaseModel):
    """Binary score for relevance check on retrieved documents."""

    binary_score: bool = Field(
        description="Documents are relevant to the question, 'yes' or 'no'"
    )


async def retrieval_grader(document: Document, question: str):
    llm = ChatOpenAI(api_key=api_key, model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)
    structured_llm_grader = llm.with_structured_output(GradeDocuments)

    system = """You are a grader assessing relevance of a retrieved document to a user question. 

    If the document contains keyword(s) or semantic meaning related to the question, grade it as relevant.

    Give a binary score 'yes' or 'no' score to indicate whether the document is relevant to the question. 

    if the document is relevant, give it a score 'yes', otherwise give it a score 'no'
    """

    grade_prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages(
        [
            ("system", system),
            ("human", "Retrieved document: 

 {document} User question: {question}"),

        ]
    )

    retrieval_grader = grade_prompt | structured_llm_grader
    grade = await retrieval_grader.ainvoke({"document": document, "question": question})

    return grade.binary_score

The code defines a structured output, builds a system and human prompt, then chains prompt, model and parser, and finally returns a clean boolean relevance score.

4. Semantic RAG with PineCone

The following figure illustrates the workflows of semantic RAG.

4.1. Ingestion Workflow

Ingestion consists of the following steps:

  1. Upload PDF to FastAPI

2. Extract text

3. Split into chunks

4. Embed chunks

5. Store vector in PineCone

4.2 Retrieval Workflow

  1. Convert user question into an embedding vector
  2. Retrieve top-K similar chunks
  3. Pass question and retrieved chunks as the context to LLM
  4. Return generated answer

4.3. VectorService Class

We defined VectorService class in service.py to expose functions for data processing, ingestion and retrival.

4.3.1. Initialization

from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain_pinecone import PineconeVectorStore

class VectorService:
    def __init__(self, index_name: str = "knowledgebase"):
        self.index_name = index_name

        # Embedding model
        self.embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small", api_key=api_key)

        # Pinecone vectorstore wrapper
        self.vectorstore = PineconeVectorStore(
            index_name=index_name,
            embedding=self.embeddings,
            pinecone_api_key=pinecone_key,
        )

        # Retriever
        self.retriever = self.vectorstore.as_retriever(
            search_type="similarity",
            search_kwargs={"k": 3}
        )

        # Text splitter (LangChain-native)
        self.splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
            chunk_size=512,
            chunk_overlap=50,
            separators=["

", "
", ".", " ", ""]
        )

Chunk size is critical for retrieval quality. If the size is too large, you dilute meaning because several topics might be assigned in one chunk. If the chunk size is too small, you lose the context of the content. Usually, set up a chunk size of 500–1000 tokens with 10% - 20% of chunk overlap. This is to ensure each chunk has appropriate context of its neighbouring chunks.

4.3.2. Store File Content

    async def store_file_content_in_db(self, filepath: str) -> None:
        """
        Read the uploaded text file, split the file, embed chunks and save chunks to vector database
        :param filepath: filepath to load to vectordb
        :return: None
        """
        logger.debug(f"Loading file: {filepath}")

        # Load entire file (safe for most RAG use cases)
        async with aiofiles.open(filepath, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            raw_text = await f.read()

        # Minimal cleaning (preserve structure)
        raw_text = raw_text.replace("
", "")

        # Split into LangChain Documents
        docs = self.splitter.create_documents(
            [raw_text],
            metadatas=[{"source": os.path.basename(filepath)}]
        )

        logger.debug(f"Storing {len(docs)} chunks into Pinecone")

        # Ingest into Pinecone
        PineconeVectorStore.from_documents(
            documents=docs,
            embedding=self.embeddings,
            index_name=self.index_name,
            pinecone_api_key=pinecone_key,
        )

This normalize newlines, splits text, and ingests chunks.

4.3.3. Search Documents

    async def search_documents(self, query: str) -> list[Document]:
        logger.debug(f"Searching for: {query}")
        return self.retriever.invoke(query)

This is simple and efficient.

5. FastAPI Backend

5.1. File Uploader

We used aiofiles for async writes

upload.py

async def save_file(file: UploadFile) -> str:
    """
    accept a UploadFile from FastAPI and save the file in specified location
    :param file: UploadFile specified by users from fastAPI interface
    :return: path of the saved file
    """
    await makedirs("uploads", exist_ok=True)
    filepath = os.path.join("uploads", file.filename)
    async with aiofiles.open(filepath, "wb") as f:
        while chunk := await file.read(DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE):
            await f.write(chunk)
    return filepath

5.2. Request/Response Models

schema.py

class RAGRequest(BaseModel):
    prompt: str

class RAGResponse(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    num_original_documents: int

5.3. Answer Generation Endpoint

Injects the RAG pipeline via FastAPI dependencies.

# dependencies.py
from fastapi import Body, HTTPException
from schemas import RAGRequest
from nodes import generate

async def get_generation(body: RAGRequest=Body(...)) -> dict:
    try:
        generation = await generate(body.prompt)

        return {
            "answer": generation.get("generation", ""),
            "num_original_documents": generation.get("num_original_documents", 0)
        }
    except Exception as e:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=str(e))

# main.py
@app.post("/generate_text", response_model=RAGResponse)
async def query_by_RAG_controller(generation: dict = Depends(get_generation)) -> RAGResponse:
    return RAGResponse(**generation)

5.4. Background Processing

FastAPI BackgroundTasks ensures ingestion happens asynchronously without blocking the event loop.

main.py

@app.post("/upload")
async def file_upload_controller(
        file: Annotated[UploadFile, File(description="Uploaded PDF documents")],
        bg_text_processor: BackgroundTasks,
):
    if file.content_type != "application/pdf":
        raise HTTPException(
            detail=f"Only uploading PDF documents are supported",
            status_code=status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST,
        )
    try:
        filepath = await save_file(file)
        bg_text_processor.add_task(pdf_text_extractor, filepath)
        bg_text_processor.add_task(
            vector_service.store_file_content_in_db,
            filepath.replace("pdf", "txt")
        )
    except Exception as e:
        raise HTTPException(
            detail=f"An error occurred while saving file - Error: {e}",
            status_code=status.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
        )
    return {"filename": file.filename, "message": "File uploaded successfully"}

6. Streamlit Frontend

A Streamlit frontend was implemented in client.py

6.1. File Upload

st.write("Upload a file to FastAPI")
file = st.file_uploader("Choose a file", type=["pdf"])

if st.button("Submit"):
    if file is not None:
        files = {"file": (file.name, file, file.type)}
        response = requests.post("http://localhost:8000/upload", files=files)
        st.write(response.text)
    else:
        st.write("No file uploaded.")
  • initializes a file uploader
  • checks if a file is uploaded when “Submit” button is clicked, and uploads the file to FastAPI

6.2. Conversation History

Maintains conversation history in st.session_state.messages

if "messages" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.messages = []

for message in st.session_state.messages:
    with st.chat_message(message["role"]):
        st.markdown(message["content"])

6.3. Chat Workflow

if prompt := st.chat_input("Write your prompt in this input field"):
    st.session_state.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": prompt})

    with st.chat_message("user"):
        st.text(prompt)

    question = prompt

    response = requests.post(
        f"http://localhost:8000/generate_text",
        json={"prompt": question}
    )
    response.raise_for_status()

    response_json = response.json()
    answer = response_json["answer"]
    st.session_state.messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": answer})

    with st.chat_message("assistant"):
        st.markdown(answer)
  • appends user input as a user message and sends it to FastAPI endpoint
  • adds the response as an assistant’s message and displays the answer

7. Colsing Summary

In this first part of the Agentic AI with LangChain series, we built a complete Semantic RAG pipeline:

  • LCEL chains for structured LLM logic
  • PineCone ingestion and retrieval
  • FastAPI backend for file upload and Q&A
  • Streamlit chatbot frontend

In the next article, we will introduce LangGraph to orchestrate multi-step agentic workflows, reduce hallucinations, and validate generated answers.

item.title: VRAM Is Zero-Sum: Why Quantization and KV Cache Are Not Rivals in Production LLM Serving
item.content:encoded:
I keep seeing the same argument surface in inference engineering threads: that KV cache optimization has made weight quantization obsolete.

I have watched teams make expensive infrastructure decisions based on this framing: choosing between the two rather than composing them.

This blog is an attempt to kill that false choice with arithmetic.

If we run an unquantized Llama-3–70B model in standard FP16 weights, even when optimizing your activation footprint with an FP8 quantized KV cache across a dual-H100 node, the infrastructure will choke at just 12 concurrent users before performance degrades into latency hell.

But if we quantize those same base weights to INT4 while maintaining that FP8 KV cache, that exact same silicon can scale to a theoretical maximum of 92 concurrent users.

Even after accounting for PagedAttention’s scheduling overhead and memory fragmentation, real-world headroom settles at a highly stable ~88% utilization ceiling, boosting concurrent user capacity by nearly 8x ($92 / 12 approx 7.7x) using the exact same hardware.

The standard counter-argument assumes that quantization inevitably destroys benchmark performance. But the math tells a different story.

This point of view is an expensive misunderstanding of production bottlenecks.

When scaling multi-turn AI systems like real-time streaming voice agents or conversational RAG, the memory wall is not a theoretical abstract; it is a hard cap on business margins.

Choosing between weight quantization and KV cache optimization is a false choice. In a high-throughput, latency-critical stack, they are tightly bound. If you don’t utilize both, you are either bottlenecking concurrency or setting compute budgets on fire.

Normalizing the VRAM Sandbox: 2x H100s (160GB)

To understand this and make an honest architectural comparison, let’s normalize the hardware footprints.

We are deploying Llama-3–70B on a standard dual-GPU cluster node consisting of two 80GB Nvidia H100s using Tensor Parallelism (TP = 2), giving us a fixed pool of 160GB VRAM.

Total VRAM allocation follows a strict zero-sum equation:

As detailed in industry sizing standards like DigitalOcean’s vLLM GPU configuration guides, reducing weight precision from FP16 to INT4 cuts memory usage by 75%, while an FP8 KV cache halves the per-token activation memory requirement on the same hardware.

Here’s what that allocation looks like across the exact same hardware footprint:

  • The FP16 Baseline: The unquantized model weights consume 140GB. After accounting for roughly 4GB of runtime engine overhead across both cards, we have exactly 16GB remaining for the KV cache allocation pool.
  • The FP8 Reality: Quantizing weights to FP8 drops the model weight footprint to 70GB, leaving 86GB for the KV cache pool.
  • The INT4 Frontier: Compressing down to INT4 brings model weights down to 35GB, leaving a massive 121GB entirely dedicated to caching concurrent tokens.

Translating VRAM into Production Capacity

For Llama-3–70B, the KV cache footprint is mathematically defined by its native architecture: 80 layers, 8 KV heads (utilizing Grouped-Query Attention), and a head dimension of 128.

Using an FP8 quantized KV cache as our baseline to compress activation memory down to 1 byte per element, the memory footprint per token works out to:

For a multi-turn assistant where the average active context window (including system prompts, conversational history, and retrieved context blocks) sits at 8,000 tokens per user, we calculate our true node capacity:

The FP8 Middle Ground: A Half-Measure

  • While shifting to an FP8 weight baseline doubles the available VRAM pool to roughly 86GB, it remains a transitional compromise for high-throughput streaming architectures.
  • Leaving nearly half of premium silicon memory tied up in static base weights is an expensive bottleneck.
  • To truly break the memory wall and maximize node density, we have to cross the sub-byte threshold into the INT4 frontier.

What Happens at the Limit?

  • When user number 13 connects to the FP16 baseline node, the engine doesn’t throw a hard Out-Of-Memory (OOM) error.
  • Thanks to continuous batching and scheduling algorithms, the engine will preempt active requests, pausing generation or placing incoming tokens into an execution queue.
  • In our production workloads, PagedAttention’s block allocation and scheduling overhead mean real-world concurrent capacity typically runs roughly 10–15% below the theoretical maximum derived from raw VRAM math.
  • Out in the real world, “queuing” translates directly to massive spikes in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) and agonizing, stuttering pauses in generation.
  • Quantization isn’t a trade-off that harms user experience, it is the exact mechanism that prevents your service from degrading into latency hell under load.

Streaming Voice and Multi-Turn Friction

Where this architectural synergy becomes a life-or-death engineering problem is inside low-latency, streaming pipelines such as conversational voice agents.

Consistent with industry targets from low-latency speech leaders like Deepgram and ElevenLabs, we are typically aiming for a total turnaround latency budget of less than 500ms, meaning inter-token latency (ITL) must stay under 20ms to keep the audio from stuttering.

1. Prefill and the Cache-Hit Reality

The initial prefill phase is heavily compute-bound because the GPU has to process the entire incoming block at once. Standard KV caching does nothing for our TTFT here.

Many engineers treat Prefix Caching as a magic bullet, assuming that because the engine can hash incoming tokens to match historical states in the KV pool, TTFT drops to zero.

But prefix caching only saves us on an exact token match (a cache hit). On a brand-new conversation or a novel prompt, we suffer a cold start, blowing past our 200ms budget.

To beat this, we must build predictive context pre-warming. My recommendation for production voice pipelines is to make the Orchestrator predictive, not reactive.
  • In our internal architectures, we address this by implementing a custom graph-traversal routing layer that I call Shadow Walk.
  • Instead of waiting for a complete user prompt, this component uses early VAD (Voice Activity Detection) increments mid-utterance to predict intent boundaries.
  • Once a path is identified with high confidence, often 150–200ms before the user finishes speaking, the orchestrator speculatively prefetches and pre-warms anticipated historical context states into the vLLM pool, masking the cold-start prefill cost entirely within natural speech pauses.

2. Decoding and Weight Quantization

Once the prefill phase lands, we enter the auto-regressive decoding phase, which is strictly memory-bandwidth bound.

To generate a single token, the GPU must stream the full weight payload through its memory hierarchy, layer by layer, on every single decode step.

  • Where the unquantized baseline requires streaming 140GB per decode step, moving to an INT4 configuration slashes that data transfer payload down to just 35GB.
  • While a 4x size reduction theoretically implies a 4x speedup, vLLM’s H100 benchmarks show ITL that varies significantly with batch size and sequence length.
  • However, in our observed production workloads at moderate batch sizes, this optimization shifts our decoding performance from an unquantized baseline of ~40ms down to a stable 16ms–20ms ITL range.
  • In streaming voice applications, this reduction is what keeps inter-token delivery speeds ahead of the audio buffer, almost entirely eliminating downstream stuttering.

Steelmanning the Counter-Argument: Where Quantization Fails

The anti-quantization crowd isn’t entirely crazy; they are just over-indexing on an architectural edge case: massive context lengths (64k+ tokens) paired with ultra-low concurrency (Batch Size = 1).

Using our value of 164 KB per token for an FP8 quantized KV cache, a 64k window scales as follows:

At a 64k context window, the KV cache alone consumes over 10.5GB of memory for that single user.

In this specific regime, squeezing weights from FP8 to INT4 yields diminishing returns because the hardware bottleneck is entirely dominated by activation memory, not weight memory.

Furthermore, aggressive post-training quantization (PTQ) introduces real reasoning degradation.

While dropping from FP16 down to INT4 via advanced techniques like AWQ or AutoRound typically results in a minimal accuracy drop of less than 1–2% on standard benchmarks like MMLU (Lin et al., 2023), crossing the sub-4-bit threshold causes model perplexity to degrade drastically.

As documented in foundational literature like SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) and LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al., 2022), LLMs exhibit “emergent features” : highly critical outlier weights that dominate specific activation channels.

These systematic outlier features emerge across all layers once a model crosses the critical ~6.7B parameter threshold, with magnitudes running up to roughly 100x larger than standard activations.

Under aggressive, uniform 3-bit quantization, these wide ranges destroy the precision of surrounding weights.

In production, this manifests as a sudden failure mode: the model breaks code syntax and hallucinates complex JSON schemas.

The Production Heuristic

Stop relying on vibe-based optimization choices. Use this decision framework based on your actual workload parameters:

The Long-Context Explorer (>32k Context, Batch Size = 1):

  • Bounded by activation footprint.
  • Run the model in FP8 or FP16 to preserve maximum reasoning capability.
  • To minimize the prefill bottleneck at these token lengths, explicitly enable Chunked Prefills combining sliding-window attention patterns with FlashAttention-3’s asynchronous Hopper pipeline to hide memory latency, rather than relying on basic weight tuning.

The Structured Engineer (Standard Context, Strict Schema/Code Tasks):

  • To guarantee your prompts don’t break API tool-calling definitions, deploy FP8 weights paired with an FP8 KV cache.
  • This maintains near-zero degradation on complex logic while doubling concurrency relative to FP16.

The Real-Time Streamer (<16k Context, High Batch Size or Streaming Voice):

  • Prioritize memory pipeline velocity.
  • Deploy INT4 weights (via AWQ/AutoRound) paired with an FP8 KV cache.
  • The freed VRAM directly drives up concurrent capacity per node, keeping inter-token delivery speeds well below the human perception of latency.

References:

  • DigitalOcean vLLM GPU Sizing & Configuration Guide
  • vLLM Blog: FP8 KV Cache on H100 Optimization Analysis
  • Lin et al., 2023 (AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression)
  • Xiao et al., 2023 (SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models)
  • Dettmers et al., 2022 (LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale)

VRAM Is Zero-Sum: Why Quantization and KV Cache Are Not Rivals in Production LLM Serving was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Database Pages: The Fundamental Unit Behind Every Query
item.content:encoded:
I was learning about sharding from first principles and exploring different sharding strategies when I stumbled upon a much more fundamental concept Database Pages.

Database Page is the smallest unit of storage management that a database engine works with to read or write data from disk.

Our SSD/HDD stores database files as raw bytes, but the database engine doesn’t read one byte at a time — that would be incredibly inefficient. Instead, it divides its data files into fixed-size blocks called pages.

  • PostgreSQL uses 8 KB pages by default.
  • MySQL (InnoDB) uses 16 KB pages (shown in the image below).

This seemingly simple design decision — reading and writing data in pages instead of individual bytes — influences how databases implement storage, caching, indexing, and query execution.

Imagine it like this…

Suppose you visit a library looking for a single quote from a book.

The librarian doesn’t tear out just that sentence — they hand you the entire book. Even if you only need one sentence, you still receive the whole book.

That’s exactly how databases work with disk reads.

What’s inside a page?

(Refer to the image below.)

  • Page Header — Stores metadata such as the page ID, checksum, free space pointer, and other internal information.
  • Rows (Tuples) — Records like Alice (id=1) and Bob (id=2), stored as binary-encoded tuples.
  • Free Space — Unused bytes reserved for future inserts and updates.

Why do databases read full pages?

Because although operating systems allow byte-level access to files, reading tiny amounts of data from disk is extremely inefficient in practice.

There are a few reasons:

  • SSDs are optimized for block-level I/O (typically around 4 KB minimum read units internally).
  • Operating systems manage memory using virtual memory pages (commonly 4 KB).
  • Reading 16 KB is only marginally more expensive than reading 1 byte, because the fixed latency of initiating a disk I/O dominates the transfer time.

So the database effectively says:

“If I’m paying the cost of a disk read anyway, I might as well fetch an entire page of useful data.”

The Buffer Pool — Pages in RAM

During normal query execution, databases operate on pages in memory, not directly on disk.

Every query follows roughly this flow:

Query arrives
      ↓
Database checks the Buffer Pool
(RAM cache of database pages)
      ↓
Is Page 5 already in memory?
├── YES → Read Carol's row directly from RAM
│         (Fast — nanoseconds)
│
└── NO  → Load Page 5 from SSD into the Buffer Pool
          Then read Carol's row
          (Slow — microseconds to milliseconds)

The Buffer Pool caches recently and frequently accessed pages.

Indexes don’t decide what stays in memory, but they reduce the number of pages a query needs to read, indirectly improving cache efficiency.

Different databases use different names for this memory area:

Why does this matter for sharding and scale?

The page model is one of the fundamental reasons why scaling databases becomes difficult.

The last point naturally leads to sharding.

Instead of storing every row of a massive table on a single machine, the table is partitioned across multiple machines using a shard key (for example, user_id).

Each shard manages its own subset of rows and organizes those rows into its own pages.

When a query arrives:

  1. The routing layer determines which shard contains the row.
  2. The B-tree index on that shard determines which page contains the row.
  3. The database loads that page into memory (if necessary) and returns the record.

Mental model:
A database is essentially a system that manages which pages live on disk, which pages stay in RAM, and which page contains the row you’re looking for.

Many of the storage and performance mechanisms inside a database — such as pages, buffer pools, indexes, and sharding — is ultimately an optimization of one question:
How do we minimise expensive disk I/O while finding the right data?

What about Redis?

Redis is one of the major exceptions.

Unlike traditional disk-based databases, Redis keeps its entire working dataset in memory.

There are no database pages to load during normal reads because the data is already in RAM.

Disk is used primarily for persistence:

  • RDB snapshots
  • AOF (Append Only File)

Since Redis serves data directly from memory, it avoids the disk I/O involved in loading pages, making it dramatically faster for many read-heavy workloads.

Final takeaway

The concept of pages is nearly universal across disk-based databases.

Whether it’s MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, or many others, they all solve the same fundamental problem:

Disk is slow. RAM is fast. Keep the hot pages in memory and minimise disk I/O.

Once you understand pages, concepts like buffer pools, indexes, query optimisation, transactions, and sharding become much easier to reason about because they’re all built on top of this idea.

That’s the foundation.

In the next post, we’ll answer an equally interesting question:

How does a database know which page contains the row we’re looking for without scanning every page?

That’s where B-Trees come in.
